before: You count up cash and card sales by hand at night.
after: Every sale is added up for you.
assumption: About 15 minutes a day matching up the day's sales.

before: Receipts pile up and you do the books in one long weekend.
after: Your sales and bills are sorted as they come in.
assumption: About 30 to 60 minutes a day of sorting and typing, spread across a month.

before: Customer names are on sticky notes and in your head.
after: Every customer is in one list you can search.
assumption: About 20 minutes a day looking things up or asking around.

before: Calls, texts and emails come in to five different places.
after: All your messages show up in one place.
assumption: About 15 minutes a day checking each place.

before: You mean to email customers, but never get to it.
after: A short message goes to past customers every week.
assumption: About 1 hour to write one message, done once or twice a month, plus the planning.

before: Happy customers leave and never post a review.
after: Every customer gets a quick, polite ask for a review.
assumption: About 15 minutes a day asking and replying, done by hand.

before: Calls go unanswered while your hands are full.
after: Every call and message gets an answer.
assumption: About 10 missed or late-returned calls a week, each costing 15 to 30 minutes of chasing.

before: Bills go out late and you chase people to pay.
after: Bills go out the same day and reminders are sent for you.
assumption: About 30 minutes a day writing, sending and chasing bills.

before: You're not sure which rules apply to you.
after: A simple checklist tells you what to do.
assumption: About 2 hours a month reading rules and answering questions.

before: You guess which days and items make money.
after: A weekly summary shows what is selling.
assumption: About 1 hour a week gathering numbers from different places.

before: You rebuild the schedule every week and work out pay by hand.
after: Shifts are filled in and pay is worked out for you.
assumption: About 2.6 hours a week building the schedule (a restaurant survey), cut by a quarter to a half by software, plus an hour or so a pay period on payroll.

before: You post jobs on many sites and teach each new hire from scratch.
after: One post reaches many sites, and new hires follow the same steps.
assumption: About 3 hours per hire in posting and repeating the same instructions.

before: Each shop does things its own way.
after: All your shops are on one screen.
assumption: About 1 hour a week per extra site chasing numbers.

before: Food prices go up and you don't know which dishes still make money.
after: You see what each dish costs and earns.
assumption: About 2 hours a month redoing costs in a spreadsheet.

before: Orders come by phone and apps, and you type each one in.
after: Online orders go straight to the kitchen.
assumption: About 15 phone or app orders a day at 2 to 3 minutes each to re-enter.

before: Bookings go in a notebook and the phone rings during service.
after: Guests book online and the waitlist runs itself.
assumption: About 20 booking calls a week at 3 to 5 minutes each.

before: You count stock by eye and food gets thrown out.
after: You see what to order and what is going to waste.
assumption: About 1 hour counting and ordering twice a week.

before: Temperature checks are on paper and often late.
after: Checks are done on a phone, and records are ready for the inspector.
assumption: About 15 minutes a day on paper logs, plus a scramble before an inspection.

before: You text each tech their jobs and change plans all day.
after: Jobs and routes show up on each tech's phone.
assumption: About 1 hour a day planning and re-planning, and fewer wasted drives.

before: You write quotes at night and forget to follow up.
after: Quotes go out from the job site, and a reminder is sent if no one replies.
assumption: About 20 to 30 minutes per quote on 8 to 10 quotes a week.

before: Yearly service customers are on a list and some get missed.
after: Reminders go out and visits are booked for you.
assumption: About 20 minutes a day tracking and calling.

before: A tech drives back to the shop for a missing part.
after: You see which parts are on which truck.
assumption: About 2 extra trips a week at 30 to 60 minutes each.

before: You measure materials from the plans by hand.
after: Software reads the plans and gives you the amounts.
assumption: About 4 to 8 hours per bid by hand, cut by a half to a third.

before: Crews and jobs live on a whiteboard and in group texts.
after: One schedule shows who is where, and everyone sees changes.
assumption: About 1 hour a day answering where crews should be.

before: You chase your subs for paperwork before you pay them.
after: Paperwork from your subs is collected in one place.
assumption: About 30 minutes per sub payment on 4 to 6 payments a month.

before: Permit deadlines are in your head and in a folder.
after: Each permit has a due date and a reminder.
assumption: About 1 hour a week tracking down status.

before: You find out an item is sold out when a customer asks.
after: You get a list of what to reorder before you run out.
assumption: About 1 hour a day checking shelves and notes.

before: You keep one stock list for the shop and one for online.
after: One stock list covers both, so you never oversell.
assumption: About 30 minutes a day updating two lists.

before: You order by gut feeling and get stuck with extra.
after: Past sales suggest what to buy next.
assumption: About 1 to 2 hours a week deciding orders.

before: You order from suppliers by phone and email, with prices in a notebook.
after: Orders, prices and delivery dates are in one place.
assumption: About 30 minutes per order on 3 to 5 orders a week.

before: You update each product on every site by hand.
after: One change updates every place you sell.
assumption: About 30 to 60 minutes a day across two or three sites.

before: Deposits don't match your sales after fees and refunds.
after: Each deposit is matched to the orders in it.
assumption: About 2 to 4 hours a month, but spread out over many payouts.

before: You're not sure which states you owe tax in.
after: You see where you owe tax and what to file.
assumption: About 2 hours a month researching and filing.

before: You copy addresses into shipping sites and compare prices by hand.
after: Shipping labels print in one click at the best price.
assumption: About 2 minutes saved per order on 100 orders a week.

before: Every return is a long back-and-forth of emails.
after: Customers start returns themselves and you just approve.
assumption: About 10 minutes per return on 10 to 15 returns a week.

before: You change ads on each site and can't tell which ones pay off.
after: One screen shows what each ad earns.
assumption: About 1 hour a week checking each platform.

before: People book by phone, and some don't show up.
after: Clients book online and get reminders, so fewer miss visits.
assumption: About 20 booking calls and 3 no-shows a week.

before: Packages and punch cards are tracked on paper.
after: Packages and plans renew on their own.
assumption: About 20 minutes a day tracking visits and renewals.

before: You try to remember each client's last visit.
after: Notes and past visits show up when they book.
assumption: About 10 minutes a day looking things up or asking.

before: You work out each person's pay from a stack of receipts.
after: Commissions are totaled for you each pay period.
assumption: About 1 to 3 hours each pay period.

before: Front-desk staff spend the day on reminder calls, and some patients still miss visits.
after: Reminders go out on their own and empty slots get filled.
assumption: About 30 confirmation and recall calls a day at 2 minutes each.

before: Checking coverage and fixing rejected claims takes hours.
after: Coverage is checked before the visit and mistakes are caught before sending.
assumption: About 10 minutes per claim problem on 20 to 30 problems a week.

before: Visit notes get typed after hours.
after: Visit notes are drafted for you to check.
assumption: About 5 to 10 minutes of note-writing saved per patient.

before: You're not sure which tools are safe to use with patient information.
after: A checklist shows which tools will sign a promise to protect patient data.
assumption: About 2 hours a month researching vendors.

before: You update the calendar on every booking site and risk double bookings.
after: All your booking sites show the same open dates.
assumption: About 30 minutes a day updating calendars.

before: You change nightly rates by guessing.
after: Prices rise and fall with demand on their own.
assumption: About 1 to 2 hours a week checking local events and rates.

before: You answer the same guest questions on every app, at all hours.
after: Common questions get a quick, friendly reply.
assumption: About 10 messages a day at 3 to 5 minutes each.

before: You text cleaners after each booking and hope rooms are ready.
after: Cleaning jobs are scheduled around check-outs.
assumption: About 20 minutes per turnover on 6 to 12 turnovers a week.

before: You sort new clients through long emails and calls.
after: One form collects what you need.
assumption: About 20 minutes per inquiry on 6 to 12 inquiries a week.

before: You write each proposal from scratch and get it signed on paper.
after: You fill in a template and clients sign online.
assumption: About 30 to 60 minutes saved per proposal.

before: You rebuild your week from memory to bill clients.
after: Your time is tracked as you work and turns into bills.
assumption: About 1 hour a week of reconstructing time, plus missed hours.

before: Client files are in email and shared drives, and you chase missing papers.
after: Files are in one safe place and requests go out with a link.
assumption: About 20 minutes a day searching and chasing.

before: You keep track of who owes what in your head and in email.
after: One list shows what is due and who is doing it.
assumption: About 30 minutes a day on status questions.

before: The phone rings during the lunch rush and nobody can answer.
after: Calls about hours, menus and orders are answered for you.

before: You're on a roof or under a sink and miss a new customer's call.
after: Every call is answered and the job is booked while you work.

before: Calls from clients and subs go to voicemail while you're on site.
after: Every call is answered, and urgent ones reach you.

before: Shoppers call to ask if an item is in stock while you're at the register.
after: Stock and hours questions get answered for you.

before: Customers ask the same questions about orders and shipping all day.
after: Common questions get an instant, correct reply.

before: You can't answer the phone with a client in your chair.
after: Calls are answered and bookings are made for you.

before: The front desk is busy and patients wait on hold.
after: Routine calls are handled, so staff can focus on patients.

before: Guests call or message at all hours with the same questions.
after: Guests get a quick reply at any hour.

before: New clients call while you're in a meeting and some never call back.
after: Every caller is answered and their details are taken.

before: Happy diners leave without a word.
after: Guests get a quick ask after the meal, and replies are drafted for you.

before: A great job ends with a handshake, not a review.
after: Each finished job gets a text asking for a review.

before: Finished projects get praise in person, not online.
after: Each finished job gets a polite ask for a review.

before: Shoppers love the shop but nobody posts about it.
after: Customers get a simple ask after they buy.

before: Few buyers leave reviews, so new visitors hesitate.
after: Buyers get an ask at the right time, and reviews build trust.

before: Clients rave in the chair but don't post.
after: Each client gets a quick ask after their visit.

before: Patients are happy, but few post reviews.
after: Patients get a polite ask after a visit. No health details are shared.

before: Guests enjoy their stay but rarely leave a review.
after: Each guest gets a friendly ask at check-out.

before: Happy clients refer you but don't review you.
after: Each client gets a short, polite ask.

before: Regulars drift away and slow days stay slow.
after: A weekly message about specials brings people back.

before: Past customers forget you until something breaks.
after: Seasonal reminders bring repeat jobs.

before: You never follow up with past clients.
after: A short note keeps you in mind for the next job.

before: Customers shop once and you never reach them again.
after: You tell past customers about sales and new items.

before: Shoppers leave things in their cart and never come back.
after: A friendly reminder brings them back.

before: Clients forget to book their next visit.
after: A reminder goes out when it is time to rebook.

before: Patients skip their regular checkups.
after: Checkup reminders go out on their own.

before: Past guests don't think of you for their next trip.
after: A note about open dates reaches past guests.

before: Past clients forget you offer more than one service.
after: A short update reminds them how you can help.

before: Catering and supplier bills get lost in the shuffle.
after: Bills go out on time and you see who owes you.

before: You write invoices back at the shop days after the job.
after: The invoice goes out from the job site the same day.

before: Progress bills go out late and money comes in slowly.
after: Bills go out on schedule and reminders are sent for you.

before: You chase business customers for payment by phone.
after: Reminders go out on their own.

before: You bill wholesale and custom orders by hand.
after: Invoices are made and sent for you.

before: Deposits and packages are tracked on paper.
after: Payments are collected when clients book.

before: Patient balances sit unpaid.
after: Statements go out and reminders follow.

before: You collect deposits and balances by hand.
after: Payments are requested automatically.

before: Invoices go out at the end of the month and clients pay late.
after: Invoices go out right away, with reminders.

before: You build the weekly schedule from texts and swap requests.
after: Shifts, swaps and pay are handled in one place.

before: Hours from the field come in on scraps of paper.
after: Techs clock in on a phone and pay uses those hours.

before: You collect crew hours by hand and work out pay at the end of the week.
after: Crews clock in on site and pay is ready.

before: You rebuild the shifts every week around who is off.
after: The schedule is made from everyone's availability.

before: You track pay for part-time and contract help in a spreadsheet.
after: Hours and pay are tracked together.

before: You juggle chair time and staff hours each week.
after: The schedule follows the bookings, and pay follows the hours.

before: You piece together staff cover around the patient schedule.
after: Shifts line up with appointments and payroll is automatic.

before: You manage housekeeping and front-desk shifts by text.
after: Shifts and pay are in one place.

before: You track staff hours and time off by hand.
after: Hours, time off and pay are in one place.
